# The Geometry of Heartbreak

In a realm where lines and angles governed the affairs of the heart, there once lived a little Square who had fallen desperately, hopelessly in love. The object of his affection was a Triangle—vivacious, sharp-edged, and utterly flirtatious—who delighted in the power she held over her devoted admirer. She kept him in a perpetual state of uncertainty, offering just enough warmth to keep him hoping, yet never enough commitment to let him rest easy. She would incline toward him one day, only to turn cold and distant the next, and the poor Square, blinded by devotion, mistook her capriciousness for a kind of promise.

Despite this maddening dance of advance and retreat, the Square nursed a quiet, persistent dream. He imagined a modest life with the Triangle at his side—a small home built of straight lines and honest angles, where they might raise a family of their own. He pictured little Squares toddling about, and perhaps a few Triangles too, inheriting their mother's sharp wit and their father's steady nature. He was not naive about the difficulties such a union might bring; he understood well enough that a Square and a Triangle might quarrel over the shape of their days, or struggle to reconcile their different geometries. But love, as it often does, made him undaunted. He believed that whatever domestic troubles might arise, they would face them together, and that would be enough.

Then, one fateful day, everything changed. Into this two-dimensional world strode a Cube—bold, imposing, and radiating a haughty confidence that no flat figure could hope to match. Where the Square offered simplicity, the Cube offered depth. Where the Square could only present four modest sides, the Cube revealed six, each one a testament to a dimension the Square could scarcely comprehend. The Triangle, ever drawn to novelty and grandeur, was utterly captivated. The Cube swept her off her feet with an ease that seemed almost cruel, and beside his magnificent three-dimensional presence, the poor Square appeared laughably small, flat, and insufficient—a mere sketch next to a sculpture.

The transformation in the Triangle was immediate and complete. All her lingering attention to the Square evaporated, replaced by dazzled fascination with her new suitor. The Square watched, powerless, as his dreams collapsed around him like a poorly drawn diagram. The humiliation of being so thoroughly outclassed, combined with the shattering of every hope he had nurtured, proved more than his simple heart could bear. In time, he withered away entirely, dying of heartbreak and despair, his four corners folding in on a grief too large for his small frame to contain.

The Cube, meanwhile, faced no such tragedy. He pursued the Triangle with the same confidence that had first captured her attention, and it was not long before he won her hand entirely. Their marriage was celebrated as a triumph of dimension over flatness, and the Triangle stepped eagerly into a life she could never have imagined before—one filled with depth, shadow, and possibility.

As for the Square, he was not mourned for long. The Triangle, now thoroughly enchanted by her new existence, forgot him with a completeness that would have broken his heart all over again, had it still been beating. She settled contentedly into her three-dimensional life, bearing children with the Cube—little Pyramids who inherited both her sharp angles and his solid depth. In this new world of volume and shadow, the memory of the devoted little Square who had once loved her so faithfully faded away entirely, as if he had never existed at all—a flat and forgotten footnote in the Triangle's rise into the wondrous, dimensional world she now called home.

# The Square's Lament: A Flatland Tragedy

In the vast plane of Euclidia, where all beings lived out their lives in perfect two-dimensionality, there existed a Square named Quadratus—honest, symmetrical, and utterly, hopelessly lonely. Each of his four sides was equal, each of his angles a dependable ninety degrees. He was, by any reasonable geometric standard, a solid citizen.

For years, Quadratus had admired Trigona from afar—a vivacious, sharp-angled Triangle whose acute charm made every polygon in the plane stop and stare. She was quick, she was clever, and she had a way of tilting her vertices that suggested she knew exactly how fetching she looked from any angle.

One golden afternoon, as the sun (a perfect Circle, as always) cast long shadows across the plane, Quadratus finally gathered his courage.

"Trigona," he said, his voice trembling along all four of his equal sides, "I have long admired your angles. Would you consider... a union? I dream of a quiet life—a modest rectangular home, some Little Squares to call our own, perhaps a small garden of parallelograms."

Trigona's three points sparkled with amusement. "How very *stable* of you, Quadratus," she said, in a tone that could have meant anything.

She did not say no. And so, in the way of the hopeful, Quadratus allowed himself to believe.

---

But the plane of Euclidia was not as simple as it seemed. For beyond the second dimension, in realms unimaginable to flat beings, there existed Cubus—a being of terrifying, magnificent depth. Where Quadratus had four sides, Cubus had six faces. Where Quadratus had a mere area, Cubus possessed *volume*. He did not simply exist in the plane; he passed through it, casting impossible shadows, appearing and vanishing with the swagger of one who knew he belonged to a higher order of reality.

When Cubus first intersected the plane near Trigona, he did not introduce himself so much as *reveal* himself—his cross-section shifting hypnotically from square to hexagon and back, a geometric striptease that left every polygon in the vicinity dizzy.

"You," Trigona said, forgetting entirely about Quadratus, "are not from around here."

"I am from everywhere," Cubus said smoothly, "and nowhere. I contain dimensions you cannot even name."

Trigona's angles fluttered.

---

Quadratus watched it happen from a modest distance—watched Trigona's vertices turn toward Cubus like sunflowers toward a brighter, more voluminous sun. He watched her laugh at jokes with punchlines that existed partially outside the plane, jokes he could never fully understand, let alone tell.

"He has *depth*," Trigona explained to Quadratus one evening, not unkindly, but not kindly either. "You must understand. I need someone who contains multitudes. Who casts a shadow. You're very... flat, Quadratus."

"I have always been flat," Quadratus said quietly. "You knew this."

"Yes," Trigona said. "But I didn't know there was an alternative."

---

The wedding of Trigona and Cubus was the social event of the plane. Cubus arrived by partially intersecting the wedding venue, which everyone agreed was devastatingly elegant. Trigona wore her finest angles. Even the Circles wept with joy, their perfect circumferences trembling.

Quadratus was not invited, but he came anyway, watching from beyond the edge of the gathering, a flat shadow of grief among the celebration.

He returned home to his modest four walls—walls that had once seemed sufficient, even comfortable, but now felt like a cage of predictable geometry. He sat with his equal sides and his reliable angles, and he thought about dimension, and depth, and all the things he would never be able to offer.

Slowly, quietly, without any fanfare or drama befitting a lesser shape, Quadratus's angles began to soften. His sides, once so precisely equal, began to waver. He was, the physicians of the plane would later note, dying of a condition with no proper geometric name—something between a collapse and a dissolution, a heart that had simply run out of dimensions to occupy.

By the time the wedding festivities ended, Quadratus had ceased to hold his shape at all.

---

They say that in Euclidia, this is simply how things go. The earnest, dependable shapes—offering their honest area, their reliable angles, their modest dreams of parallelogram gardens—rarely compete with those who arrive from beyond, trailing impossible shadows and the seductive promise of *more*.

Trigona and Cubus lived, by all accounts, quite happily—she delighted by his depths, he amused by her sharp wit, both entirely unbothered by the flat, forgotten shape who had loved her first, and loved her simply, and had nothing to offer but the honest, unglamorous geometry of himself.

And that, the old shapes of the plane would tell you, was never going to be enough.

# The Square and What Lies There

There is a square in the heart of the old town, and it has watched centuries pass beneath its worn cobblestones. There, generations have gathered—to celebrate, to mourn, to simply exist together in shared space.

The square is bordered by buildings of varying ages, each one telling a different chapter of the town's story. Some structures date back hundreds of years, their facades weathered but proud, while others are newer additions that blend, sometimes awkwardly, with their older neighbors. And yet, despite these differences in age and architecture, there is a harmony to the whole—a sense that everything belongs precisely where it stands.

In the mornings, there is a particular quality of light that falls across the square, illuminating the fountain at its center and casting long shadows from the surrounding buildings. Vendors arrive early, setting up their stalls with practiced efficiency, and the air fills with the mingling scents of fresh bread, flowers, and morning coffee.

By midday, the square transforms. There are children playing near the fountain, their laughter echoing off stone walls. Elderly residents occupy the benches they've claimed for years, watching the world pass by with quiet contentment. And tourists, cameras in hand, pause to capture what locals have long since stopped noticing—the intricate details carved into ancient stonework, the particular way sunlight catches the fountain's spray.

Evening brings yet another mood. There is a softness to the square as lanterns flicker on and restaurants extend their seating into the open air. Conversations blend with distant music, and the day's heat gives way to cooler air that seems to invite lingering.

The square remains constant, and yet it never truly stays the same. There is always something new to notice, some small detail previously overlooked. Perhaps this is what makes such spaces essential to a town's identity—they hold history and present moment simultaneously, offering both continuity and change to anyone willing to simply be there, and to look.

# Square's Sorrow

There once was a Square, quite boxy and true,
Who fell hard for a Triangle—oh, what a view!
Three sides so sharp, so pointy, so keen,
The most dashing shape that he'd ever seen.

He'd roll himself over (which squares shouldn't do),
Just to bring her fresh circles of morning dew.
He wrote her love notes in perfect right angles,
"My love for you never bends or untangles!"

He said, "Triangle, darling, my four-cornered heart
Beats only for you, we should never part!
Your acute little points make my geometry spin,
Let's be parallel forever, through thick and through thin!"

She giggled and blushed (at a perfect 60 degree),
"Oh Square, you're so sweet, but there's something to see..."
Then in through the door, with a swagger so smooth,
Came a Cube—third dimension—with nothing to prove.

"I've got depth," said the Cube, "I'm a Square, but with MORE!
I'm the upgrade, the sequel, the shape you adore!"
He winked with a corner (he had eight, quite a lot),
And Triangle swooned at this six-sided plot.

"Oh Square, I am sorry, but he's got more sides,
Well, technically faces—there's more he provides!
He's got volume, dimension, he's stereo, he's deep,
While you're flat and simple—no offense, but I'll keep

My heart for a shape that can properly spin,
Who casts real shadows and has more within!"
So she left with the Cube in a three-dimensional bliss,
Leaving poor Square with just memory of that kiss.

Now Square sits alone, feeling flat and depressed,
"Two dimensions ain't much," he sadly confessed.
But a Rectangle winked from across the school hall...
Cheer up, little Square—you're not doomed after all!

For love in the shape-world is never quite square,
It's got angles and corners you don't see, but they're there.
So here's to the broken-hearted, geometric and true—
Even when Cubes steal your girl, there's a shape out there for you!

# The Shape Cotillion

In Geometria, land of lines,
where curves and angles paid their tines,
the annual ball of Shapes convened
beneath a sky of graph-paper green.

Sir Square arrived with corners pressed,
"I'm never obtuse," he'd oft confessed,
"I keep my angles right, you see—
ninety degrees of dignity."

But Acute Triangle, sharp and small,
was the belle of the geometric ball,
"I may be pointy," she'd softly say,
"but I'm quite the *acute* one, come what may!"

Old Circle rolled in without a care,
no corners, edges, anywhere—
"I've got no sides to speak of, true,
but I'm well-*rounded*, through and through!"

Then Rhombus swaggered, rather slanted,
"My angles aren't what you'd have wanted,
I lean this way, I lean that,
but at least I'm never falling flat!"

The Cube showed up—a real big deal,
Square's cousin, with volumetric appeal,
"I've got that extra *thickness* now,
I'm not flat like Square, somehow!
While he's stuck living in the plane,
I've got depth—it's not the same!"

Square sniffed, "Well *excuse* my dimension,
some of us prefer flat convention!
Not every shape needs to be thick—
I'm perfectly happy, two-D, and slick."

Then Cone arrived, quite pointed too,
"I'm sharp on top, but round all through,
a mixture rare, both smooth and keen—
the most *complex* shape you've ever seen!"

Line Segment came, so straight and thin,
"I've got no width to speak of—akin
to nothing at all in the space I fill,
but I'm the shortest distance still!"

Poor Obtuse Angle hung by the wall,
too wide and lazy to join the ball,
"I'm over ninety, don't you know,
too spread out for the dance, I'm slow."

But Right Angle winked, "Don't be obtuse—
er, I mean, don't self-abuse!
Come dance with us, forget your measure,
every angle brings its pleasure!"

So Circle spun and Square did prance,
and Rhombus led a slanted dance,
while Cube boasted of his mass,
and Cone twirled with acute-angled sass.

And as the geometric ball wound down,
each shape returned to their part of town—
flat or solid, curved or straight,
each one perfect, each one great.

For in this land of lines and space,
no single form could claim first place—
some had *thickness*, some were thin,
but all belonged, and all fit in.
